title: Cuba: human suffering, political stalemate and the need for coordinated action
label: 19 October 2026 · Cuba: humanitarian and political crisis
summary: Witnesses described a fast-worsening, largely man-made disaster in Cuba driven by an oil blockade, hyperinflation and institutional collapse. Basic services—food, water, power, healthcare and transport—are failing, hitting the elderly, children, Afro-Cubans and those without relatives abroad hardest. Aid is arriving but is fragmented and slowed by bureaucracy and fuel shortages. The panel warned that neither a popular uprising nor a simple external fix is likely, and urged coordinated international humanitarian relief and diplomatic mediation, with the UK playing a leading role.

chapters.title: What people on the streets are living through
chapters.takeaway: Daily life in Cuba has collapsed for many: pensions are worthless, rations are gone, disease and crime are rising, while a small private sector grows rich.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: Can you describe the current situation in Cuba, and how stable the Government is?

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: On the streets it's brutal. About 40% of people have virtually nothing: elderly on tiny pensions, ration shops empty, and many now begging or searching rubbish.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Another 40% get money from relatives abroad, while roughly 20% work for or own MIPYMEs—private businesses that have grown fast and created wealth for a few.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Doctors and teachers are still on state pay; people bring small gifts to hospitals. Education is collapsing because graduates can earn much more in the private sector.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Basic services are failing: piles of rubbish, rising petty crime, frequent blackouts, and irregular water supplies sold by street vendors.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Health risks are rising: dengue, Zika and chikungunya are back, and waterborne diseases like hepatitis A and dysentery are becoming common—cholera is possible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned 'MIPYMEs'—that's private small and medium businesses that have appeared since reforms.

chapters.title: Humanitarian needs and what the WFP is doing
chapters.takeaway: The World Food Programme is active in Cuba but faces funding, shipping and fuel problems that limit its reach; coordinated aid and exemptions are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lena, what's the World Food Programme seeing and doing on the ground?

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: WFP has worked in Cuba since 1963. Our current programme is about $35m a year; we reached 1.5 million people in 2026 but face a $10m shortfall.

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: Cuba imports 80–85% of its food. Fuel shortages are disrupting local production, transport and distribution. The libreta ration system now only targets the most vulnerable.

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: Vulnerable groups include the elderly, pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, and people with chronic illness or disabilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can the WFP bring in fuel and distribute it directly?

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: Humanitarian food is exempt from sanctions, but over-compliance by carriers causes delays. We can buy fuel from private suppliers in Cuba, but it's costly and irregular.

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: We urge partners to use diplomatic channels to speed exemptions and to support logistics, especially ahead of El Niño drought risks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who funds you on Cuba?

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: Support has come from Korea, Sweden, the UK (a £1m contribution after Hurricane Melissa), Canada, the EU and others, but more resources are needed.

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: I must leave now, but to be clear: unless fuel and import routes improve, humanitarian need will rise fast and widely.

chapters.title: How Cubans see the crisis, and who they blame
chapters.takeaway: Most Cubans blame their own Government for failing services, though the US blockade is a decisive factor; mass emigration has reduced the chance of a popular uprising.

turns.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale
turns.text: Who do ordinary Cubans blame, and is the Government secure?

turns.speaker: Dr Hansing
turns.text: People are angry at their Government for not doing more. The crisis is a 'polycrisis'—economic, social, political and psychological—and Afro-Cubans are harder hit because they often lack relatives abroad.

turns.speaker: Dr Hansing
turns.text: Data from Cuba is unreliable; some numbers suggest infant mortality and maternal deaths have risen, and possibly 60% living in extreme poverty, but conditions may be worse than official figures show.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: Most Cubans want change and blame their Government, but the Government has survived decades of pressure and retains tight control. A mass uprising like in Eastern Europe is unlikely because many young people have left.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Vanderbilt's survey had 79% blaming the Government, though it used internet polling. In my own conversations, most people I spoke to blamed their Government rather than abroad.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: Two million-plus have emigrated since 2021; that exodus removes a portion of the population that might otherwise push for big change at home.

turns.speaker: Dr Hansing
turns.text: There is a generational split: some younger people hoped for US intervention, while older people prefer diplomatic solutions but feel abandoned materially.

chapters.title: The role of the US embargo, sanctions and possible interventions
chapters.takeaway: The US embargo (codified in law) and recent oil restrictions have worsened the crisis; some US exemptions and private imports exist, but intervention carries big risks and uncertain effects.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How have US policies shaped this, and could the US intervene militarily?

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: The embargo is law (the Libertad Act) with strict conditions for lifting it. Recent US moves—an oil blockade and tighter sanctions—have intensified the crisis.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Is US fuel getting into Cuba through middlemen and exemptions?

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Yes. There are US imports and middlemen operating under licences; some companies have exemptions to sell fuel to private actors in Cuba. But that doesn't solve nationwide blackouts.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: Trump-era policy aimed to squeeze the regime to induce a collapse or defections. That strategy is risky and flawed: the regime is resilient and may not crumble as intended.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: If the state collapses, the risk is a failed state near US shores, with possible narco-trafficking and migration crises—big security concerns for the region.

turns.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale
turns.text: Would Cubans welcome US intervention?

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Some say they would, but many Cubans I talk to do not want military intervention; they fear the consequences. Intervention risks unknown violence and long-term instability.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: Politically, US actors like Marco Rubio and Trump may want change for domestic reasons, so some form of action is possible politically, but practical and moral costs would be high.

chapters.title: What the international community—and the UK—can do now
chapters.takeaway: Panel urged coordinated humanitarian aid, diplomatic mediation led by a coalition (including the UK), maintaining an embassy and supporting Cuban public services to avoid collapse.

turns.speaker: Dan Carden
turns.text: Could the UK use diplomacy to make humanitarian access easier?

turns.speaker: Dr Hansing
turns.text: Yes. We need two tracks: urgent, coordinated humanitarian assistance and a diplomatic push to reduce US-Cuba confrontation. The UK could lead a coalition with Europe, Canada and Latin America.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: Working via CARICOM, Commonwealth countries and regional powers could de-politicise the response and focus on relief and mediation rather than a US–Cuba duel.

turns.speaker: Ruaridh Nicoll
turns.text: Practically, the UK should keep a functioning embassy, support education and hospitals, and fund direct aid rather than short visits with suitcases of donations that can look performative.

turns.speaker: Lena Savelli
turns.text: From the WFP side: facilitate humanitarian exemptions, fund logistics and fuel, and shore up contingency planning for El Niño-driven droughts. Donor funds are urgently needed.

turns.speaker: Dr Hansing
turns.text: If things worsen—disease outbreaks, children dying or mass departures by sea—we could face a refugee crisis. That should motivate early coordinated action.

turns.speaker: Dr Sabatini
turns.text: A negotiated, staged approach is realistic: international mediation, humanitarian corridors and planning for post-crisis reconstruction so external investment doesn't swamp Cuban public needs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We'll press for diplomatic engagement, speak to regional partners, and consider following up with US contacts when we visit. This has been a timely and powerful briefing.
